report:
**Conclusion: Unsupported.** There is no reliable clinical evidence that capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans, and it should not be used in place of established oncology care.

The breast-cancer findings commonly cited are **preclinical**: for example, capsaicin reduced viability and migration and caused cell-cycle arrest in the MDA‑MB‑231 breast-cancer *cell line*. Effects in cultured cells do not establish an effective or safe dose, benefit, or survival effect in patients.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33173974/

Broader scientific reviews conclude that oral capsaicin as a complement to chemotherapy remains speculative; cancer-related effects may also vary by dose, tissue, and biological context.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/

Human breast-cancer-related capsaicin research found in the literature concerns **symptom management**, such as topical treatment of post-mastectomy pain—not treatment of the malignancy itself.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2780073/

By contrast, the National Cancer Institute describes evidence-based breast-cancer care as combinations of surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, and other indicated systemic treatments; capsaicin is not listed as a breast-cancer therapy.  
https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/hp/breast-treatment-pdq

Patients considering capsaicin supplements or topical products should discuss them with their oncology team, particularly during active treatment.
